newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan activist says opposition party losing ideal.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan activist says opposition party losing ideal.

text.p: Taiwan's leading pro-independence activist on Wednesday accused the island's largest opposition party of losing its ideals, forsaking right for might and becoming a "satellite" of the ruling party it aims to replace.

Peng Ming-min, a former presidential candidate for the Democratic Progressive Party, said his party had degenerated into a power-hungry group that no longer fought for Taiwan's sovereignty and democratic rights against rival China.
"The current leadership of the Democratic Progressive Party has lost ideals and the party is finished as a real opposition party," Peng said in an interview with Reuters.
"The Democratic Progressive Party has become a satellite o,f the (ruling) Nationalist Party," the 72-year-old Peng said.

A dissident who spent 23 years in exile during Taiwan's martial law era, Peng scoffed at party chairman Hsu Hsin-liang's stance that Taiwan already was an independent country and therefore sovereignty was no longer an issue.
"That kind of talk is sheer nonsense. Our constitution still says that Taiwan is part of China and our government still calls itself the Republic of China government," Peng said.

"Our school textbooks devote many more pages to Chinese history and geography than to Taiwanese history and geography. The government's perspective is still that China is superior to Taiwan," he added.

Taiwan and China split after the Nationalists lost a civil war to the Chinese communists in 1949 and took refuge on the island. Both Taipei and Beijing say they want to reunify eventually, but disagree sharply on the terms.

The Democratic Progressive Party, whose political emergence in the 1980s helped end the Nationalists' authoritarian rule, contends Taiwan is an independent country and reunification is an outdated goal.

The opposition party's activism helped launch Taiwan into a democratic transformation that culminated with its first direct presidential election in March 1996. Peng was the party's nominee in that election, which the Nationalists' incumbent President Lee Teng-hui won in a landslide.

Peng's election defeat led to the resignation of former party chairman Shih Ming-teh, and Hsu has said subsequently that the party needs to alter its public perception as a radical interest group in order to expand its power base.

In particular, political analysts say, the party has softened its position on the sovereignty issue in order to appeal to mainstream voters who are wary of China's threat to attack if Taiwan declares independence.
China mounted intimidating war games in waters near Taiwan before the island's March election in what Beijing admitted was an attempt to dissuade people from voting for pro-independence candidates.
Peng has refused to compromise on the sovereignty issue and accused the opposition party leadership of practising "ideological corruption".

"A political party is supposed to lead and educate people, not just go along with what is popular. Yes, it is important for a party to try and get power. But the way it gets power is more important," Peng said.
"The Democratic Progressive Party had a goal and it abandoned that goal. That is ideological corruption," he said.
